speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house is already aware of the great loss which its membership sustained on Friday last by the death of the hon. member for Bonaventure, Hon. Charles Marcil. The adjournment of this house on Friday evening was an impressive collective tribute on the part of hon. members to the memory of one who had attended forty consecutive sessions of this parliament, and who in point of service was its oldest member. This morning the citizens

of the capital and many from other parts of the country joined with hon. members of both houses in paying a further tribute of respect to the memory of him who had become so familiar a figure in the public life of our country. The press, of all shades of political thought, have united in expressions of appreciation of Mr. Marcil's many years of public service. The tributes thus expressed have been supplemented by others from former political opponents as well as personal and political friends and by the clergy of the church of which he was so devout a member.
In these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, my purpose in rising this afternoon is primarily that of gratefully acknowledging what has already been said by way of tribute to the memory of our late fellow member, and of saying, on behalf of those who knew him best, how worthy he was of the eulogies which have been expressed. Mr. Marcil's public life in Canada is generally known to all who are here assembled. I imagine that what our own and future generations will regard as of surpassing interest in his long career is the link which it affords between a past which is rapidly receding and a future which is certain to be full of change.
The Hon. Charles Marcil came of a family nine generations of which had lived in the province of Quebec and of which ten generations extend over three centuries. He was born in Ste. Scholastique on July 1. 1S60. Like the late Hon. Peter Veniot, his deskmate for a period, to whom tribute was paid only a few days ago, he was one of the very few remaining members of this parliament who were born prior to confederation and who, from memory, could recall incidents associated with that great event. He was one of another group, somewhat larger but also much too rapidly disappearing who sat in this house with the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
With Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Mr. Marcil was privileged to enjoy a close personal as well as political friendship. There was much in the lives of Mr. Marcil and Sir Wilfrid Laurier which made the association between them natural as well as close. Both, as I have said already of Mr. Marcil, came of families that for many generations had lived in the province of Quebec. The early careers of each had its association with journalism, each came to devote his entire time to politics. Both Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Marcil were endowed by nature with real distinction in appearance which their habit of thought and manner of life, as the years went by, continued greatly to refine. Both were gifted as writers and speakers, and each spoke with equal fluency in the French or the English

The Late Hon. Charles Marcil
language. I doubt if anyone who had not heard Mr. Marcil in his prime can imagine with what freedom and grace he spoke alike in French and in English. He was, I think, at his best depicting a scene from the romantic background of our country's history, or foreshadowing the greatness of Canada's future as he conceived it would become. He was a true Canadian, with great faith in Canada and the place Canada would come to hold among the nations of the world. That faith, throughout his life, he ever sought to impress upon his fellow countrymen. He was an ardent Liberal, strong in his convictions, but always moderate and tolerant in the manner in which he spoke. Like Sir Wilfrid, he exhibited at all times those attributes of courtesy and chivalry so characteristic of the race and generation to which each belonged. It was a part of Mr. March's contribution to the parliament of our day that when he presided over the proceedings of this chamber or participated in its debates he was true not only to the Laurier tradition in his point of view but, expressed himself in the Laurier manner with grace and dignity.
An estimate of Mr. Marcil's contribution to the life and work of this parliament would require perusal of its records and debates over forty sessions. To such a degree did he enjoy the unbroken confidence of his constituents that he was elected by them to ten consecutive parliaments. With the exception of two instances, so far as I have been able to ascertain, this record has not been surpassed. I believe Sir Wilfrid Laurier himself and the late Hon. John Haggart each sat in this House of Commons through eleven parliaments.
Mr. Marcil's return on so many occasions was a well deserved record of confidence and one which reflected equal credit upon his constituents. Last night I took occasion to glance through the pages of Hansard of the previous session in order to see what Mr. Marcil had said on the last occasion on which he spoke in this chamber. It was not. surprising to discover that his last word was one of grateful acknowledgment to a minister of the crown for something the minister had been able to do which was of assistance to the constituency represented by Mr. Marcil and to adjoining constituencies. Confidence akin to that so fully given to Mr. Marcil by his constituents was also expressed in a very real way by his fellow members in this house of commons who elected him successively to the position of deputy Speaker and chairman of committees in 1905, and to that of Speaker in 1909, a recognition which was further emphasized by his appointment in 1911 as a member of the privy council of Canada. During the last four parliaments his fellow members of
the Liberal party chose him as permanent chairman of the party caucus. In the course of his long life of public service, there was much else in the way of recognition of his abilities and attainments by municipalities, representative organizations, societies, univerities and by governments in our own and other countries.
Mr. Marcil was in his 77th year. For a life so full of service, of achievement and of well merited recognition, there surely can be either for him or for us no occasion for regret that he was taken away while still a member of the House of Commons and its oldest member in point of service. We shall miss the benefit of his long experience and wise counsel in parliamentary affairs, but to have had his faculties unimpaired to the end, and to have been spared the infirmities, disappointments and decline which too often are the accompaniment of advancing years is something which of itself is in the nature of a benediction, and something we should not begrudge him who has been taken from us.
It was his to enjoy the fulfilment of the ancient promise-
"Thou shalt come to thy grave in a full age Like a shock of corn cometh in in his season."
As one whose life's endeavours were thus rewarded, his name will hold an honoured place in the history of this parliament, and his memory will continue to be cherished by all who knew him.
Mr. Speaker, this house will look to your Honour to convey to Mrs. Marcil and other members of the family an expression of its sincere and deep sympathy in their bereavement.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are reminded by what has been said, as well as by our own observation and experience, that the hand of death is ever with us. My first expression is one of deep regret that this house has lost the knowledge and experience of one who was its dean in point of service.
With respect to the character and extent of the service rendered by our late comrade and fellow member, I can add nothing to what has been said by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). To have been a member of the house during ten parliaments is an almost unique experience. Indeed he was a connecting link between the nineteenth and twentieth centuries; for he was elected Speaker of the house before most of us had a seat in the chamber. His life is a history of the years from 1900 to 1936.
I should like, too, to express my sincere sympathy to the right hon. the leader of the government, to his colleagues and the sup-
The Late Hon. Charles Marcil

porters of his administration, in the loss they have sustained both collectively and individually. They have lost a faithful friend, a warm supporter, a devoted follower, and a worthy exponent of the principles of Liberalism as he saw them. Faithful in the discharge of his duties, he was ever mindful of the claims of those who lived in the Gaspe peninsula. Those of us who have listened to him in the house will realize that while his convictions were strong he spoke but seldom, and expressed them in terms both moderate and persuasive.
Obviously it is not for one situated as I am to speak with any degree of authority as to the value and extent of the service he rendered to his party, and through it to the country. But I can say that on the other side of his life, that side we describe as citizenship, his example was of the first order. By precept he created for himself an influence which cannot readily be estimated. Sometimes it is difficult to appraise the value of public service. Opinions clash, criticism is keen, antagonisms are great, and regard for human frailty is not very evident. But when we come to consider the life of one who was a citizen of the community and occupied a public place, I think we are well within the mark when we say that by precept and example Mr. Marcil's life must stand as an influence to younger men not only of this day but of the generations which have come into the world during the time he lived among us. He was courteous; he was kind; he was considerate of others; he was unselfish; he was generous to a fault, and, within limits, he was most tolerant. He had that inward peace which is reflected in the outward man. His countenance indicated that quietness of mind which rises superior to all philosophic doubts or scientific dogma. He was devout, intensely so; he believed in religion as a practical living and moving force. He practised it, and the influence of his example among younger men cannot fail to have had a very marked effect among those with whom he came in contact.
These attributes were known to us all, whether he was our close personal friend, our political associate or otherwise known to us. Those of us who sometimes saw that courtly smile always received it as almost a benediction. I think I can say nothing that would more clearly indicate the impression his life has made upon mankind than the words I have just spoken. If ever there was among those whom I have known in the House of Commons and elsewhere one who seemed to me to give a fair answer to that 
age-old question, a question that concerns us all-"And what doth the Lord require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?"-it was Charles Marcil, whose passing we so greatly deplore.
Speaking for those associated with me, I trust the leader of the house will convey to the sorrowing relatives he has left behind an expression of our deep and sincere regret at the great loss they have sustained.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to add my personal tribute to those which the prime minister and the leader of the opposition have just paid to the memory of our late lamented fellow-member. Hon. Mr. Marcil was the only member of this parliament who was in the house in 1904, when I came heTe for the first time. I knew him previously, for he was one of the public speakers whose eloquence had thrilled my youth. His melodious voice, his phrase which seemed to flow harmoniously like a clear and beautiful stream, his imposing and dignified presence made him a favourite speaker among the people. Sir Wilfrid Laurier once told me that he knew of no Canadian who had so perfectly mastered the two official languages of this country. During thirty-three years, I sat at his side, and it is with deep emotion that I bear testimony to his having always been a devoted friend, a loyal colleague and a wise counsellor. Owing to his extreme kindness he could not have enemies. " Charlie " Marcil never hated anybody. Nothing could ever impair his equanimity and natural recti-tude._ He gave all his intellect, all his heart, all his life to his country, to his friends, and to _ the principles he held dear. Intensely religious, as it has just been pointed out, he was a model of piety, charity and devotedness. He was a great Canadian.
To Mrs. Marcil and the other members of his family, to his faithful constituents in Bona-venture, I wish particularly to tender the sympathies of the French Canadian members of this house.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to add my poor tribute to the dear dead colleague whose passing we to-day mourn. He was my friend and intimate, and I think it is probably true to say that at the time of his death I was his oldest living friend. It was in 1879, fifty-eight years ago, that he began his journalistic career on the staff of the Montreal Gazette, with which paper I had been associated since June, 1874. My recollection is

The Late Hon. Charles Marcil
that Mr. Marcil as a youngster-he was then only nineteen years of age-had a great flair for politics. He began life as an adherent of the Conservative party, and his earlier speeches on the public platform were delivered in the cause of that party. Not many years thereafter, from convictions the sincerity of which no man who knew Charlie Marcil will for a moment doubt, he changed his party allegiance. Throughout the rest of his life it can be said that he was a consistent and stalwart member and supporter of the Liberal cause.
His attainments were great. He was distinguished in many ways. He not only served his country in this House of Commons, but he served the city in which he lived, Montreal, first as a member of the city council and subsequently as one of the commissioners to whom the management of the city was entrusted. Summing up his character in a word, one can say of him that he was a gentleman.
The duration of his public life is almost unexampled. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) referred to two other men in public life, Mr. John Haggart and Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who sat in parliament for perhaps as long a period as did Mr. Marcil. Of course the outstanding example of public service in parliament was that of Macdonald, who sat for forty-seven consecutive sessions, first in the legislature of the old province of Canada and then in this House of Commons. In a way the greatest tribute that has been or can be paid to Mr. Marcil is the fact that during the nearly thirty-seven years in which he was a member of this house he represented the same constituency, which is at once a tribute to his integrity, his character, his kindliness, and his ability. He was a most fluent speaker, as has been said, in both languages. Having had an Irish mother he probably lisped English at his mother's knee, but doubtless he would call himself, because of his ancestors through a long line, a French-Canadian, as he was in heart and spirit. He was a broad-minded man. I would not call him a partisan; I think that would be an unfair term to apply to Charlie Marcil. I would call him a moderate Liberal. He was always ready to give and take, and any opponent who may have crossed swords with him or differed from him in discussion would at least have agreed that he was fair in the maintenance of his views, and would have concluded that discussion with an esteem and respect and even an affection for Mr. Marcil.
I have said that as a young man campaigning in the good old province of Quebec he
made a reputation as an orator. I know as a matter of fact, and he was no mean judge, that the late Sir Adolphe Chapleau, regarded Mr. Marcil as one of the rising young men of Canada, an appreciation that has been fully justified.
Let me just say this in conclusion. If it can be said of any man it can be said of Charlie Marcil that-
He had kept
The whiteness of his soul, and thus men o'er him wept.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is certainly not necessary that anything more should be said, but we in this group would like to associate ourselves with the tributes of respect that have been paid and to offer our very deep sympathy to those whom our late colleague has left behind him. The distinguished bearing and finely chiselled features of Mr. Marcil marked him out, I think, in almost any company, and, further than that, they seemed to indicate a certain spiritual quality not very common. I had thought, in trying to sum up the impression Mr. Marcil had made upon us, rather of the words just uttered by the hon. member for St. Antoine-West-mount (Mr. White)-he was a gentleman; and I think I might add-and I do in all respect- a gentleman of the old school. We shall all miss him.

Mr. Speaker, judging from the manifest sincerity of the words of esteem with which previous speakers have praised the life of the late Mr. Marcil, and of the tone in which they were uttered, I deem it a privilege to join my voice with those who have already honoured him. It has been written: Blessed is he who has found his work; let him seek no greater blessedness. This man evidently had found his work, and ably he did it. During much of my life I have felt that one of the greatest blessings would be that of having the privilege of dying in harness. Mr. Marcil was blessed thus, and it can therefore be said that he has been blessed both in his living and in his dying. Our group rejoices to honour such a man.

That a select special committee of the house he appointed to continue and complete an inquiry begun by the standing committee on agriculture and colonization, pursuant to a resolution of the house on March 2, 1936, into the causes underlying the high prices of farm implements, with particular reference to the advance in prices in the year 1936.
That the said select special committee shall have the power to send for persons, papers and records, to examine witnesses under oath, and to report from time to time.
That the said select special committee be authorized to engage the services of counsel, auditors, technical advisers, clerks, stenographers and investigators to aid and assist the said committee in the inquiry, and to print the evidence, proceedings and documents received by the committee.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE
subsubtopic: INTO HIGH PRICES WITH PARTICULAR REFERENCE TO INCREASES FOR 1936
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for reasons that I made quite clear last session I do not agree with the steps that are being taken, but it is sufficient to say that; for it is quite evident that the government desires to proceed in this way, and having sufficient numbers to enable it to do so, that is the end of it. I think an inquiry of another kind would have been very much better than an inquiry before a political committee. I think it would be very much better to have a non-party body-not partisan but non-party-judicial or otherwise, than a committee of this house, to consider a matter that will lend itself to so much acrimonious discussion. I assume it was for that reason that the government selected a judge rather than a committee of this house to investigate textile matters. I believe that that is a much sounder method, but since the government has decided to proceed with a committee, I think the motion itself is hardly ample so far as the last paragraph is concerned. It is a motion to continue an investigation that has already been partly carried out, and it is not sufficient to say that what has already been done should be made available to the committee; it should be provided that what has been taken in the way of records

shall become part of the records of the continuing committee. Simply to make it available does not enable the committee to utilize it for the purpose of predicating findings upon it. It should become part of the records of the new committee. I shall content myself with making this observation, but I cannot think that the end sought will be accomplished as effectively as it would be by the utilization of the other method. Had that been done, the inquiry might have been carried on during the recess and the results made available to parliament, which is hardly possible now so far as this session is concerned.

Mr. W. K. ESLING (Kootenay West) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 13 to amend the Copyright Amendment Act, 1931.

Will the hon. member
explain?

By this bill it is sought to amend two sections of the Copyright Act which refer only to musical works. Hon. members will recall that the Canadian Performing Right Society exercises authority under the statute to issue licences and to collect fees in compensation for the use of

Copyright Amendment Act
music which the society claims to control. As a matter of fact it assumes control of between two and three million titles. It assumes control of almost everything that is on the air, and when, an applicant for a licence suggests to the society that it should give him a list of the titles to which it claims control, it simply replies with a statement that the society does not have to furnish such a list and that the applicant can get the information by going to the copyright office in Ottawa. This is not a very satisfactory response to an applicant in, we will say, Saskatoon or Prince Rupert or some far distant community, and the purpose of one of the amendments is to require the Canadian Performing Right Society to furnish to each applicant a list, certified to by the Secretary of State, showing that the society is in actual possesion or control of the titles to music in respect of which it attempts to collect a fee.
As to the other amendment, under the tariff just revised by the copyright appeal board the various broadcasting stations throughout the dominion will pay to the Canadian Performing Right Society the sum of $70,000, which covers fees for receiving sets known as domestic receiving sets. I assume that to mean that they are receiving sets in private homes. But there is a special licence and special fee required from stores, skating rinks, lodge halls, hotels, restaurants, cabarets and like places; this speacial fee is fixed at a minimum of five dollars, with accumulations and conditions making gradual increases to a maximum which is uncertain. These establishments contend that, in view of the fact that the broadcasting stations pay such generous licence fees to the performing right society, a second tax by way of a special radio license fee is unjust. The second amendment therefore seeks to exempt stores, skating rinks, hotels, restaurants and such small establishments from a second radio tax.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: What is the exact text of the short findings of the federal royal commission on technical education, appointed by Sir Wilfrid Laurier s government, to the effect that technical education was exclusively a federal problem under the British North America Act?

subtopic: ROYAL COMMISSION ON INDUSTRIAL TRAINING AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION
speechtext:
The exact text of the findings of the royal commission on Industrial Training and Technical Education, 1913, under the chairmanship of Dr. J. W. Robertson, C.M.G., is set out in sessional paper No. 191d of the Journals of the House of Commons, 1913, but is not to the effect that technical education was _ exclusively a federal problem under the British North America Act. The commission's opinion as to control and regulation is expressed in the following extract, from page 21 of the said sessional paper:-	_ _
"The commission is of the opinion that, industrial training and technical education in order to be of greatest benefit to individuals, to industrial development, to localities, to the several provinces and to the dominion as

Questions
a whole, should be organized and maintained in accordance with the following principles:-
"1. It should be under provincial control and regulation.
"2. It should receive financial support from individuals, from local authorities, from provincial governments and from the dominion."
The commission's opinion as to federal participation in technical education is to be found in the following extract from page 26 of the same sessional paper:-
"5. The very considerable increase in the population of Canada by immigration is throwing additional burdens for elementary education upon the communities and the provinces. The enhanced public revenues due to growth by immigration goes in a large measure into the dominion exchequer. The increase of the volume of trade brings in larger amounts through the customs oifices. This would indicate that the new financial responsibility and burdens for industrial training and technical education, on a scale large enough and generous enough to be available to all the people between the ages of 14 and 18, should be sustained in large measure by funds from the Dominion government."
The commission's recommendation in regard to the extent of the financial assistance which should be rendered by the federal government to the provinces is set out on page 268 of the said sessional paper, as follows:-
" The commission recommends that the sum of 83,000,000 be provided annually for a period of ten years by the parliament of Canada and paid annually into a dominion development fund."

subtopic: PROCEDURE WITH RESPECT TO QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY AND PARLIAMENTARY RETURNS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROCEDURE WITH RESPECT TO QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY AND PARLIAMENTARY RETURNS
speechtext:
On Friday last the hon. member for Weybum (Mr. Douglas) asked a question of my colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) as to whether the government had any intention of introducing a certain bill at this session. The Minister of Justice replied that, in the absence of the leader of the government, the question would have to stand. I may say to my hon. friend, in answer to his question, that the matter is one of policy and therefore if any action is to be taken it will be made known by the government in due course. However, I am rising at the moment more particularly to direct the attention of hon. members to the rules of the house with respect to questions. Standing order 44 reads:
(1)	Questions may be placed on the order paper seeking information from the ministers of the crown relating to public affairs; and from other members relating to any bill, motion, or other public matter connected w-ith the business of the house, in which such members may be concerned; but in putting any such question or in replying to the same no argument or opinion is to be offered, nor any facts stated, except so far as may be necessary to explain the same. And in answering any such question the matter to which the same refers shall not be debated.
(2)	(a) Any member who requires an oral
answer to his question may distinguish it by an asterisk.	,
(b) If a member does not distinguish his question by an asterisk, the minister to whom the question is addressed hands the answer to the Clerk of the House, who causes it to be printed in the official reports of the debates.
Standing order 45 has also to do with notices of questions and matters of that sort. I wish to point out that the rules have been framed for the convenience of members and for the saving of the time of the House of Commons. The question that was asked by the hon. member might have been put as a notice on the order paper and it would have been replied to in the regular way. If he had wished an oral reply all he would have had to do was to distinguish it by an asterisk. But to rise and ask a question orally in the house and in the absence of the minister concerned to expect another minister to answer it is simply to take up the time of the house to no good purpose. May I respectfully say that I have noticed during this session that many hon.

Business of the House-Procedure
members are falling into the habit of handing to members of the government, just prior to the time at which the house convenes, questions to which they expect ministers to make verbal replies. This procedure is all right where the matter is urgent and it is clearly in the public interest that the question should be asked at the moment, and where some interest would suffer if it were not then asked; but with that exception, I think it would be in accord with the wish of hon. members in all parts of the house that the rule with respect to giving adequate notice of questions should be followed.

subtopic: PROCEDURE WITH RESPECT TO QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY AND PARLIAMENTARY RETURNS
speechtext: May I say a word in reply to the Prime Minister? I sent a copy of the question to the Prime Minister forty-eight hours before asking it, and on the morning of the day I asked the question the Prime Minister's secretary telephoned me and said that in view of the fact that the Prime Minister would not be in the house he had arranged with the Minister of Justice to answer it. He telephoned me this morning and said that he had misunderstood the Minister of Justice. I gave the minister sufficient notice and if I had known that he preferred that I should put the question on the order paper I would have followed that procedure.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROCEDURE WITH RESPECT TO QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY AND PARLIAMENTARY RETURNS
speechtext:
What my hon. friend has just said only proves the wisdom of the rule. If my hon. friend had sent the question to the Clerk of the House it would have appeared on the order paper and an answer would have been ready. It so happened that on Friday it was impossible for me to be here at the opening and I thought I had arranged to anticipate any matters which might come up. I raise the point, not by way of criticism of my hon. friend but merely to bring forward a course of procedure to which I think the attention of the house should be drawn with a view to saving unnecessary repetition in questions of the kind. May I at the same time say a word about some of the information and returns which are being asked for. The government has every desire to give to the house all information that is desired. But some requests are made that involve a large expenditure, an expenditure far out of proportion to any end that might be served by the information requested. I would suggest that where members have requests of the kind to make of the government they take up with the minister concerned in the first instance the possibility of securing the information, and that they consider carefully the form in which requests are worded. For example, on today's list
there is question No. 48, relating to civil servants. The question reads:
1.	How many civil servants entered the various departments of the government under the provisions of the Civil Service Act, since 1920?
2.	What wTas their place of residence when they entered the service?
3.	How many are bilingual in each department?
That means a search from one end of Canada to the other for the information which is requested. subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, in view of the urgent necessity of effective action for the improvement of the social and economic conditions of the people of Canada, and, in view of the condition of social and other legislation passed by parliament during the tenure of office of the late government, and, in view of the forward-looking legislation recently enacted in the United States and other democratic countries, a special select standing committee of the house be set up to recommend the specific amendments to the British North America Act required to enable this dominion parliament to enact necessary and desirable legislation for the better social conditions of the Canadian people.
He said: Mr. Speaker, since the resolution was placed on the order paper when the house met in January, the subject matter of the resolution has become of more than academic interest. Of course last Tuesday's debate, initiated by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), to a great extent anticipated a discussion of the matter now before us. But since that time the judgments of the privy council with respect to social security measures of the late government have been delivered, and they create something in the nature of a national emergency in relation to the whole question of social and economic legislation. People find their wills thwarted by constitutional difficulties undreamed of when the British North America Act was passed.
To-day Canada finds herself definitely unable to enact progressive social legislation on a national scale through a national parliament, and thereby a situation of national concern and emergency is created. Apart from any argument as to the desirability or otherwise of the legislation affected by the judgments, it is imperative that in days when
democracy is being undermined ways and means shall be found at once to rectify the situation and to restore to the Canadian people their faith in our democratic institutions as instruments of reform. In my opinion this involves both a short term and a long term view. To meet the latter the resolution was originally placed upon the order paper. To meet the former it seems to me that without delay, now that the dominion jurisdiction has been denied, an interprovincial conference should be summoned to consider what measures should be taken to protect and improve standards of living. With parliament in session and the legislatures either sitting or about to sit, the situation might be met temporarily by the passage of concurrent legislation. It seems to me however that because it is both cumbersome and unsatisfactory, this should be regarded as only a temporary method of dealing with matters of the kind.
I am pleased to note that the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act has been declared valid, and I trust no attempt will be made to restrict its terms or provisions, indeed if anything is done regarding this measure, I hope its terms and provisions will be widened rather than narrowed. Of the measures disallowed several are of fundamental social and economic importance. Who will deny, for example, that uniform legislation for the regulation of hours of industry, the weekly day of rest and the setting of minimum wages, is necessary? Conditions exposed in some industries by recent investigations cry aloud for immediate legislative action.
What about unemployment insurance? If, as we are frequently told, business is on the upswing, then immediate preparation should be made for the inevitable downward plunge, the time to make that preparation is when economic conditions are said to be improving. The same consideration would apply with equal force to legislation and plans for the orderly marketing of our farmers' produce. Such legislation should have the approval of the producers. In the opinion of many people -and I can speak at least for those in western Canada-a natural products marketing act is a primary necessity. My submission is that failure to provide such measures of social security will invite widespread discontent and seriously undermine public confidence in parliamentary institutions. Hence the recent judgments of the privy council may become the source of further grave unrest, unless steps are taken by parliament and the legislatures to give effect to the demands of farmers and workers for social legislation and security
B.N.A. Act-Mr. Coldwell

measures. Whatever else may be contemplated, it seems to me an emergency inters provincial conference should be called immediately to deal with the situation which has arisen as a result of the privy council judgments.
Having said that, may I add that when I placed the resolution on the order paper I intended, first, to focus attention upon amendments to the British North America Act and, second, to discuss proposals designed to give greater social and economic security to the masses of the Canadian people. During nearly twenty years of active participation in public affairs, in common with others I have supported various suggested reforms which almost invariably in their initial presentations have been met by the argument that they could not be undertaken because of the British North America Act. I was one who perhaps regarded the argument rather more lightly than events of the past week might have warranted. This act, which is the cornerstone of our constitution. I fear has become at times a pillar behind which reactionary interests have sought to shelter and to hide. Proposals have been made recently for the appointment of a royal commission to investigate economic and other conditions in western Canada. I believe the suggestion has much to commend it. but I would point out that in view of the judgments just delivered we need, first of all, to amend or remodel the British North America Act in order to be able to make effective any recommendations of such a royal commission.
Perhaps because of my old country education and training in the rights and duties of British citizenship I find it very difficult to understand the profound reverence for written constitutions and documents which I have found in many quarters in the country in which I now live. Possibly this arises out of our susceptibility to ideas emanating from south of the Canada-United States border, where the constitution of 1776 has been regarded as almost too sacred to be criticized. I am glad to note that in the discussion which occurred in this house last Tuesday there did not seem to be a disposition to regard the British North America Act in a similar light.
Parliament is elected by the .people to carry out the will of the people as expressed from time to time. It is intolerable that men, no matter how wise and how good they may have been in their day and generation, or parliaments long since gone by, should be able to bind the hands of a new generation and of their successors. Recently we have heard much about the supremacy of parliament. Under British constitutional practice
rMr. Coldwell.]
the House of Commons in that country is, in the finanl analysis, the supreme power. If there were previously any doubts as to this, I take it that the events surrounding the abdication of King Edward VIII settled the matter once and for all. Therefore I believe an attempt should be made here, in Canada, to deal with our constitution so that it cannot be used as a drag upon the progress of the Canadian people. Morever, unless we bring it more into conformity with the requirements of our age, its inflexibility, like the rigidity of a sealed container full of air when heat is applied, will sooner or later cause an explosion. If we look over our economic and social situation at the present time we shall find many factors generating heat and making for such an explosion.
As was indicated the other afternoon, the British North America Act is a relic of the pre-industrial age. Some people have called it the ox cart age, but "pre-industrial age" I think describes it more accurately. The chaotic conditions of the dominion-provincial financial arrangements illustrate how out of date the act has become in the field of modern social and economic requirements. There can be no permanent or satisfactory adjustment in these relationships until we come to grips with the social and economic problems involved in the constitution. I venture to say that there is not a member of this parliament or a public man in Canada who has not felt at some time or other that the constitutional question has been used as a drag upon Canadian progress.
However well it suited the requirements of 1S67 it is no longer a satisfactory instrument for the completely changed conditions of 1937. The seventy years which have elapsed have seen a world more completely transformed than did the thousand years which preceded them. Let me emphasize the fact that the British North America Act constricts our activities, makes for confusion, and encourages sectionalism and general instability. Public discussion and consideration of this aspect of our constitution must accompany proposals for measures leading to greater economic and social security. That is why this resolution has been placed upon the order paper. I said a moment ago that under the British constitution the House of Commons is, in the final analysis, the supreme authority. It is time we brought our constitutional practice into conformity with that of Great Britain.

speechtext:
The leader of the
opposition (Mr. Bennett) says, "parliament, not the House of Commons." But I was just coming to that point. In my opinion the House of Commons is, in the final analysis, the supreme authority under British parliamentary practice. For example, I can see no good reason for the continued existence of the senate, which was established ostensibly to protect provincial rights but which I believe no longer does so. If the abolition of the senate is not considered by such a committee as the one I have in mind, then the question of an elective senate might be considered. We should at least bring our parliamentary practice into conformity with the practice in Great Britain. In that country when a bill has been passed by the House of Commons and turned down by the House of Lords in two consecutive sessions, it becomes law without the consent of the upper chamber when it is passed by the House of Commons in the third consecutive session.

subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext: Do you think provincial legislatures should be continued and sustained?

subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Yes, I do. I think there is a place for the provincial legislatures, just as I think there is a place under the British unitary system for local self-government on the county plan although they are not analogous. However, if we are to have a parliament legislating on social and economic matters for the people of Canada, a divided authority on the same matters is a very dangerous thing and is likely to lead to dissatisfaction and unrest among the people. I am simply suggesting that this committee should consider the Parliament Act of Great Britain, as passed in 1911, and study ways and means of providing legislation of a similar sort for Canada.
It may be said: how can these amendments be made effective? I think that the fathers of confederation, who were silent on that particular matter in the legislation which created this federal parliament, clearly contemplated that any amendment to the British North America Act or the constitution of Canada would be a matter for legislation on the part of the imperial parliament. In my opinion that was distinctly a colonial idea and one which prevailed in what might be called colonial days. I believe Canada should have the right to amend her own constitution. I was reading Professor Keith's treatise on the King and the Imperial Crown. In discussing the Statute of Westminster at page
428 he indicates very clearly that Canada did not desire that particular power when the statute was under discussion. He says this:
The views of Canada were decisively in favour of retention of supreme power,-
Supreme power by the British parliament.
-for as yet Canadian constitutional change in essentials depends on British legislation.
Since then in South Africa the issue has been met by enacting the Status of Union Act of 1934, which provides that no imperial act shall extend to the union unless it is extended by a union act; and secondly by the enactment of the Royal Executive Functions and Seals Act of 1934, which provides that any instrument may be signed by the governor general by the authority of the cabinet where the king's signature for any reason cannot be obtained. Since the governor general is the nominee of the government, that clearly gives the Union of South Africa power to amend its own constitution, to proclaim its neutrality, and to decide its destiny.

subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext: It had the power to amend its constitution before.

subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Thank you. In view of the confused international situation, and in conformity with our ideas of equal commonwealth status, Canada should be endowed with at least somewhat similar powers.
I would say that such a parliamentary committee as the motion suggests, should consider, first, ways and means by which the will of the Canadian people as expressed by the House of Commons can be made supreme. Since 1867 we have travelled far, and the Statute of Westminster quite definitely lays down the principle that the self-governing dominions are co-equal partners in the free association known as the British commonwealth of nations. Canada then as a nation must have the right to deal with its own social, economic and constitutional problems. If we achieve that right the problem on which the committee should make recommendations is that of the method to be followed within the structure of confederation.
I do not suggest that there should be any interference with minority rights peculiar to our national groupings. I do suggest that the time has arrived when power to legislate upon matters not contemplated when confederation was realized should be clearly defined as between this parliament and the provincial legislatures, and since the use of legislative powers usually involves financial commitments the whole question of the fields of provincial and federal taxation should be carefully reviewed. To-day we have many
B.N.A. Act

Mr. Coldxoell

instances of serious overlapping. Moreover, we have provinces that do not levy certain forms of taxation, which consequently are used as shelters to cover those who wish to escape those particular forms of taxation. I do not think that that is desirable or good or wise.
In recent years doubts regarding the respective rights of this parliament and of the legislatures have retarded the enactment and proclamation of really necessary and worthwhile legislation. Matters not contemplated when this dominion was established have become of first-class political and social importance, and necessary reform is thus unduly delayed by needless constitutional discussions, references to courts of law and subsequent judgments, resulting in discontent and widespread unrest and disaffection.
All this needs careful investigation and clarification so that no legal doubts nor unprogressive law courts can thwart the people's will. Social legislation demanded by the people remains to-day inoperative because of constitutional and legal differences of opinion, and now definitely of judgments. Until these barriers have been removed there is difficulty in securing that uniformity of action in regard to minimum wages, orderly marketing, health services, social insurance, old age pensions, and so on.
Duplication in administration involves added costs and regrettable delays in rendering the desired service to the people of the country. Action concerning matters of national interest is prevented by the lack of parliament's power to deal with them. In such matters we can proceed only as rapidly as the most reactionary provincial government will permit. Surely this is far from being a satisfactory state of affairs, and in these days it tends to discredit our democratic institutions as instruments of progress just when it is important to strengthen public confidence in them.
As I said a moment ago, we can proceed only as rapidly as the most reactionary provincial government will allow this country to proceed. I am not saying which or if any of the provincial governments may be placed in that category at the present time, but I do submit that if that point is debatable now, there may come a time when this, that, or the other province may have a reactionary government while all the other provincial governments are progressive, and under such a situation desirable legislation of a progressive nature might be held up indefinitely. In a rapidly changing world Canada lags behind already in social and economic legislation.

This I think can be largely attributed to the constitutional doubts and difficulties which I have already indicated, and to the refuge which parliament and the legislatures have taken from time to time behind the cloak of the constitution. Yet surely both bodies today realize that the problem must be dealt with. Unrest among the people of the various parts of this dominion will continue and become intensified unless we solve the problem arising out of divided jurisdiction.
Already the financial side of confederation settlements has undergone drastic, if temporary, revision. How these revisions were undertaken is a matter of recent history. But upon what basis they were made is not at all clear to the public and the provinces, or, may I suggest, to the members of this house. I find, for example, that the subsidy payments to four provinces by the dominion have been greatly augmented to such an extent that in two cases the augmentation is only slightly less than the original subsidy, while in the other two it greatly exceeds the annual subsidy. The public accounts for the year ended March 31st last reveal that the subsidy for British Columbia was $874,561.46, which under vote 209 was augmented by a special grant of $750,000. The subsidy for Prince Edward Island, $381,931.88, was augmented by a special grant of $275,000. The subsidy for New Brunswick was $693,040.16, and it was augmented by a special grant of S900.000, while the subsidy for Nova Scotia was $653,047.60, and it was augmented by a special grant of $1,300,000. Obviously there were good reasons for making these grants, but equally obviously it is difficult for the public to understand why a distressed area such as the province of British Columbia, with a large population, received so much less than Nova Scotia, with a much smaller population. I am not at the moment criticizing the justice of these grants, but I venture to say that few members of this house could explain them, and I am using them to illustrate the point that the whole question of financial relationships between the dominion and the provinces should be carefully reviewed, because, after all, to a large degree they are based upon agreements and constitutional practices.
The financing of the various social projects should also be reviewed. For example, old age pensions have now reached the point where they are becoming nation-wide; hence they should be entirely federal and more nearly uniform. Incidentally, the clause in the old age pension act permitting the authorities to take liens on the small estates of the pensioners should be repealed. As

By.A. Act-Mr. Coldwell
long as that remains, the payments are not pensions but loans repayable at death. Many old folks endure hardship and privation rather than relinquish their right to little bits of property which represent their savings of a lifetime. At the moment Canada lags behind both Great Britain and the United States in economic and social legislation, and demands for what we call social security measures will tend to increase rather than to decrease as this fact becomes more generally known and its implications realized. Hence it seems to me that preparation should be made, not next year or the year after but now,, to meet these needs by clearly defining the powers of parliament and the legislatures, and, may I add, not only the powers but the responsibility of these various bodies. That would be one of the principal tasks of such a committee as that which the resolution asks shall be set up.
Sooner or later, too, this country will have to face the problem of debt in all its forms and phases. Last week we had an opportunity of discussing the problem of increasing purchasing power, and at that time we indicated how wealth was becoming accumulated and pointed out some things that might be done to redistribute purchasing power and remove some of our debts to those who have acquired the ownership of such obligations. I do not propose to traverse any of that ground this afternoon, but simply desire to suggest that the power to reduce debt and interest must be more clearly defined. In some provinces we have two debt adjusting authorities operating under dominion and provincial statutes respectively. Endless arguments arise as to which of the two authorities or statutes is the better, and doubts and difficulties also arise in the minds of harassed people. Yet debt adjustment must continue, and since the problem is nation-wide, national consideration should be given to it.
I intended to outline at some length what other countries or dominions were doing in relation to these problems, but time does not permit me to touch more than briefly upon their legislation. We are in many respects twenty-five years behind the motherland in such measures as unemployment insurance, housing legislation, and health benefits. British legislation along these lines first came into effect in 1912, after, it should be said, some European nations had adopted somewhat similar measures. We have now the benefit of their experience, and the bitterly condemned " dole, ' as it was called, of a quarter of a century ago has earned universal approval from all save a few
reactionary persons here and there who have not realized the needs of the changed times in which we live. True, there are dark places, very dark places, in the old land, but there would have been more of them but for her social legislation. We could well afford to give effect to unemployment insurance, to schemes of housing and health services, upon a more generous and national scale. Money thus spent would, I submit, be more wisely spent than what may be expended for armaments even at the present time. More recently the United States has travelled far along the road of social security legislation, but owing to its constitution greater difficulties than we are likely to experience have had to be met. In spite of this, under the leadership of the central authority, unemployment benefits, old age pensions, pensions for the blind, the care of dependent children, and so on, are all well on the way. Our proximity to the United States makes it inevitable that increasing pressure will be brought to bear in Canada for the enactment of similar legislation. Preparatory to meeting these demands adequately a committee such as the motion proposes could recommend to this parliament appropriate legislation to enable us to meet them on a national basis.
In our sister dominions great progress has been made lately. This is especially true in New Zealand, where under a socialist administration-headed, incidentally, by the Hon. Michael Savage, and, incidentally, a gentleman who is a devout Roman Catholic-a series of progressive measures has been enacted, among them the control of the financial system through the national ownership of the central bank; the passage of a primary products marketing act so that minimum fixed prices are guaranteed from time to time and butter and other dairy produce marketed through a single government agency; measures for the prevention of profiteering, the control of hours and wages in industry, restoration of wage and pension cuts; and legislation is foreshadowed to control investment of national savings. At the close of 1936 the minister of industries and commerce for New Zealand was able to report significant rises in all departments of economic and social activity. In spite of the fact that New Zealand has grave difficulties on account of her remote position and her relatively small population, the minister was able to say that the dominion as a whole is marching towards an era of prosperity which will be reflected in higher standards of life for the masses of the people.

B.N.A. Act-Mr. Coldwell
New Zealand has been able to go forward because no constitutional difficulties lie in her path. She is a small country, not a federal union, but a legislative union-the unitary system, as it was described here the other afternoon. We have questions which arise out of our federal union which ought to be settled at once. I would therefore suggest to this house that it approve of the government establishing a committee to inquire into the constitutional changes necessary to modernize our constitutional practice. That is what the motion asks, and I feel that members who do not necessarily agree with all the suggestions I have made in support of the resolution can nevertheless support the principle of it.
The privy council decisions made public a few days ago emphasize the importance of dealing with this matter at once. From time to time we hear in this house of what are termed subversive elements in our midst, but let me point out that if we have such subversive elements, they spring and grow from bad economic and social conditions. Repression will not stamp them out. The only way we can meet the demands for the better life, and the discontent that arises from a denial of those demands, is to enact measures in the parliament of Canada that will give to men and women an opportunity not only to work but to enjoy the natural resources of the country and the benefits of the machines and of science with which we are surrounded.
May I say that this is particularly true of the younger people in our dominion. There is discontent among them, and I believe that that discontent can be either healthy or unhealthy. They have a right to live, to enjoy the blessings of home and of marriage. They have a right to make a living. To-day they are denied those privileges. Can we wonder if there is discontent? Yet, through all these years, ever since the war, when new measures have been suggested to meet the economic and social situation that has been developing, again and again these measures have been opposed on the ground that they are not constitutional. To-day we have a demonstration of the fact that some of these much needed measures have been declared by the highest court in the empire to be unconstitutional. It is therefore of primary importance that parliament at this time consider ways and means of enabling either the dominion or the provinces to enact incontestable social legislation; but I submit that you must consider these problems on a dominion-wide scale rather than from a pro-

vincial point of view. Either the dominion, or the provinces, should have the right and the power to legislate to meet the social and economic situation that exists to-day.
I see that my time is just up, and I am going to ask the house to support this resolution and the government either to accept it or to suggest an alternative which is better. If such an alternative is suggested and appears to be better than the resolution I have proposed, I shall have a great deal of pleasure in supporting it.

subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
The other afternoon a debate of this kind took place, and at that time, with my limited knowledge of the rules of the house, I thought it was entirely out of order. But nobody seemed to call Mr. Speaker's attention to the fact, possibly owing to the prominence of the hon. members who started the debate. I think it is a good thing for the house to discuss at considerable length the British North America Act and possible amendments thereto, and as there are on the order paper no fewer than three resolutions dealing with the same subject we shall have plenty of opportunity to discuss it.
In the first place, confederation was formed for two main reasons. I have heard it said that confederation was formed in the first place on account of fear, but I do not altogether agree with that. Confederation was formed for two main reasons-the purpose of defence of the then colonies, and in order that those colonies might trade freely with one another. If the fathers of confederation had had in mind some of the things that have been done since then by this parliament, confederation would never have been formed. Some eleven or twelve years after the date of confederation there was put into effect by the then government a policy that has gone far towards wrecking confederation in this country, and it may succeed in wrecking it if it goes much further. I refer to the policy of protection, or the protective tariff. Had a protective tariff been in the minds of the fathers of confederation and been spoken of at the time, certainly some of the provinces would not have joined that confederation, especially had they been able to see into the future and visualize what would happen in this dominion.
Some two or three years ago a commission was formed in Nova Scotia to determine the effect of the protective tariff on that province, or rather evidence brought before a commission went to show that certain parts of the dominion paid to the extent of about

B.N.A. Act-Mr. Ross (Moose Jaw)
twenty-five cents out of every dollar to the protected industries of the country, receiving nothing in return. The protective tariff has developed in one particular section of Canada large industries at the expense of other sections-not in a provincial way, because where that industrial area lies the provinces as a whole are not helped by it to any great extent, but certain favoured individuals in that area are assisted. This has meant that industry in Canada has been drawn largely into one part of the country and any benefits therefrom have gone to that section to the detriment of other parts of the dominion. This has greatly affected the confederation. When one realizes that the fisherman on the Atlantic coast, who is a primary producer, must turn over from a fifth to a quarter of his fish in order to uphold protected industries in Canada; that the coal miner must turn over from a fifth to a quarter of the coal he mines in order to uphold those protected industries; that the man in the woods in Quebec who hauls in pulpwood must turn over from a fifth to a fourth of his load in order that the protected industries of Canada may prosper in one small section; that the miners of the north, the lumbermen, the farmers from one end of the country to the other must do the same thing, it is hard to say that confederation, when we have such policies carried on under it, is a good thing for Canada as a whole, and Canada will not hold together if that policy continues very long.
I heard the other day a statement, by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) I believe, that there was no danger of splitting Canada at the present time. Well, I should like to tell him and the members of this house that there never was a time in the history of Canada when there was more danger in that regard than there is right now. The people in the outlying parts of the country and the provinces farther away from that protected area are becoming sick and tired of paying through the nose and getting no return, while certain favoured people in one section are benefited. There are large sections of the country that have very few ties, or ever had, with that section. And when you find that certain portions of the country are and always will be devoted to the production of primary products and therefore under such a policy always will have to pay and receive nothing in return, the danger of trouble in this country is apparent.
The protective tariff has done another thing. We set up certain kinds of taxation for the federal government and certain kinds for the .provinces. Now that under the protective system all industry has been driven
into one small portion of the country it is very difficult for many of these provinces to procure the necessary amount of money to carry on their business. For instance, the executives of all these large industries-and I would link with them the financial houses and insurance companies, which are grouped in the same parts of the country-who draw down large salaries, are required to pay income tax only in one province. An income tax is a proper tax for the provinces, under direct taxation, but many of the provinces cannot reach the people whom they should be able to tax. These people who are gathered in one small portion of the country collect much of their revenues from every part of the dominion, but they are liable for income tax only in the province in which they live.
