speechtext:
Provincially that is so. Then there is another thing. A succession duty tax is a proper tax for a province under direct taxation. If a man happens to have been successful throughout his life until, we will say, he reaches the age of fifty-five and then desires to sell his business and invest his money in this country, naturally he turns for investment to Canadian industries. If he happens to purchase stocks in the industries of Canada and dies while still owning such stocks, he can be taxed in any outside province only on the property that he owns in that province. On the stocks he has purchased, however, the succession duty tax is paid to the province in which the head office or transfer office of the industry is located. In other words the tremendous amount of money that has been invested in industries located in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec by people living in other provinces is made to pay toll, in the form of succession duty . tax, to those two provinces, while the other provinces are unable to collect that tax. We have often heard it said in this house that by far the largest portion of our taxation is collected in certain cities in eastern Canada. Of course that is so, but it is so because people in those cities are doing business with all the other parts of the country.
Everyone seems to have adopted the view that we must amend the British North America Act in certain particulars. I am not so very sure that we have to amend that act a great deal, because when the British North America Act was framed a certain field was laid out for the provinces and another field for the dominion. If many of the provinces cannot carry out the work allotted to them by the British North America Act the only
432	COMMONS
B.N.A. Act-Mr. Ross (Moose Jaw)
reason is that they are financially unable to do so. When these provinces entered confederation in the first place they were separate, sovereign states or democracies. Under the British North America Act they are still separate, sovereign states and democracies within a certain field, and this parliament has no right to encroach upon their rights, as we have done so often in the last few years. For instance, while every mode of taxation was made available to the dominion, at that time it was not anticipated that the dominion would dip into direct taxation so deeply that it would be difficult for the provinces to collect enough revenue to enable them to carry on.
Further, Mr. Speaker, in this parliament we have passed certain legislation which has been more or less coercive in regard to the provinces. In effect we have said, "Well, the people want a certain thing. We will put at the disposal of the provincial governments so much money, and let the provinces put up the rest." As a result the moment we put an act in force in this parliament saying that this government was willing to give so much money if the province put up the remainder, the people of the province invariably forced the provincial authorities to spend that money, whether or not they wanted to do so. In this way the provinces have been obliged to make expenditures at different times which they could not afford. We passed an act here in connection with technical education. We started this thing and then, after it became a costly venture, we dumped the whole proposition over on the provinces and told them to go ahead and handle it. The same thing applies to roads. It is perfectly all right, if the government wants a trans-Canada highway, for the government to go ahead and build it. They have no right to say to the provinces that they must put up a certain amount of money in connection with such a venture. In that connection the federal government coerced the provinces into spending money that they did not want to spend, and the same thing applies in connection with old age pensions. I was in this house when that measure was passed, and we had no more right to pass an old age pension act than we had to pass a good deal of the other legislation we have enacted. Again we forced the provinces into something, whether or not they wished it. As I said a moment ago, they are sovereign states; they are democracies in their own right, and in this parliament we have no right to force a province into anything which it does not want to do, at least until we amend the British North America Act.

Prior to 1867, there had been a certain amount of taxation in the four provinces which formed the confederation. At that time a certain line of work was laid out for the provinces and another line for the dominion. If we look back to that time we find that customs and excise revenue for those parts of the dominion amounted to about $8,500,000. In order that the provinces might have sufficient money to carry on the work they were to do the dominion turned back to them about $3,000,000, or almost half the amount of money then collected through customs and excise. I do not think the provinces would be in such great trouble to-day if the dominion had continued to do that. We must revamp the distribution of revenue between the provinces and the dominion.
Some people have said that the provinces have been coming down here with their hats in their hands only to get more money from the federal parliament. We should arrange matters so that they can get more of the total revenue collected than they are at present able to get. It is a crying shame that at this time, when interest rates are so low, the provinces are placed in the position that they cannot refinance the great debts they carry. No doubt in a short time interest rates will be back to normal, and the debt the provinces carry, if they can carry it, will be a tremendous load upon their shoulders.
I do not agree with the resolution because I do not think a committee of parliament can be set up to handle the matter properly. I believe there should be plenty of discussion, and each side of the question should be set forth in debate. Sooner or later some government will endeavour to arrange matters so that the provinces will get a proper portion of the total revenue collected to enable them to carry out the business the fathers of confederation entrusted to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Coldwell) who introduced the resolution spoke, as he always does, with vigour, and followed a well prepared argument. I was hoping he would give some reason which would justify the creation of a committee of the kind suggested by him.
May I review what has been done in the matter in recent years. As to the usefulness and even the necessity, under present circumstances, of amendments to the British North America Act, I think we must all agree, but I fail to see where the procedure suggested by the hon. member will be useful. Indeed I am afraid it would hurt rather than help the

B.N.A. Act-Mr. Lapointe (Quebec East)
end he has in mind. In 1935, on motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) the house adopted a resolution whereby it set up a select committee consisting of Messrs. Cowan, Guthrie, Turnbull, Ernst, Gagnon, Lapointe, Mackenzie (Vancouver Centre), Ralston, and Woodsworth-
-to study and report on the best method by which the British North America Act may be amended, so that while safeguarding the existing rights of racial and religious minorities and legitimate provincial claims to autonomy, the dominion government may be given adequate power to deal effectively with urgent economic problems which are essentially national in their scope.
Although the language of the present resolution is not quite the same, I believe the meaning is absolutely the same as the one I have set out. The committee in 1935 was appointed for the very same purpose. It sat practically all session and in the course of its proceedings heard various legal experts and professors. In order to impress the house with the fact that the committee did its work in the best possible manner, may I point out only a few of the names connected with its work. They were W. S. Edwards, K.C., Deputy Minister of Justice; Doctor O. D. Skelton, Undersecretary of State for External Affairs; M. Ollivier, K.C., Joint Law Clerk of the House of Commons; Doctor W. P. M. Kennedy, Professor of Law, University of Toronto; Doctor F. R. Scott, Professor of Law, McGill University; Doctor Norman McLeod Rogers, Professor of Political Science, Queen's University, and Doctor Arthur Beauchesne, K.C., C.M.G., LL.D.. Clerk of the House of Commons.
After discussing the matter in detail the committee adopted the following resolution:
The committee recognizes the urgent necessity for prompt consideration of amendments to the British North America Act with reference to a redistribution of legislative power and to clarify the field of taxation.
In view of that, surely we do not need to set up another committee to make the same finding. The report continues:
It is further of opinion that the conference hereafter proposed should carefully consider the adoption of a recognized yet flexible method of amendment.
In view of the fact that the several provinces did not feel it advisable to give the committee the benefit of their views with respect to the method of procedure to be followed in amending the constitution, the committee is of the opinion that before any decision upon the subject matter of the resolution is finally made, that the opinions of the provinces should be obtained otherwise if at all possible and for that reason recommends that a dominion-31111-2S
provincial conference be held as early as possible in the present year to study the subject matter of the resolution. The proposed conference should have ample time in which to study every phase of the question.
In view of the above recommendation the committee expressly refrains from recommending any form of procedure for amendment so as to leave the proposed conference entirely free in its study of the question, except that the committee is definitely of the opinion that minority rights agreed upon and granted under the provisions of the British North America Act should not be interfered with.
That was the work of the committee of 1935. In accordance with its recommendation a conference with the provinces was summoned in November and December of 1935, upon which occasion a subcommittee dealt with constitutional questions. That constitutional subconference had an agenda containing the following items:
1.	Revision of the British North America Act.
2.	A.greement on future action with reference to social legislation.
After the subconference had completed its work it adopted a resolution, which was ratified by the full conference, as follows:
This conference, in the interests of the dominion and of the provinces, is of the opinion:
(a)	That amendments to the British North America Act are now and subsequently may be necessary and imperative.
(b)	That, as in the case of all the other self-governing dominions, Canada should have the power to amend the Canadian constitution provided a method of procedure therefor satisfactory to the dominion parliament and the provincial legislatures be devised.
(c)	That the Minister of Justice convene at an early date a meeting of appropriate officials of the dominion and of the provinces to prepare a draft of such method of procedure to be submitted to a subsequent conference.
(d)	That a conference be held at an early date after such draft has been prepared to consider such a method of procedure.
This committee of experts, composed of officials of the dominion and of the provinces, was called for the purpose of doing the work assigned to it by the conference. These officials, representing most of the provinces, spent part of the session of 1936 working in Ottawa with the dominion officials. A tremendous amount of work was done; drafts were prepared and agreement was reached on many important matters which had been debated previously and in connection with which some difference existed. There are still some matters upon which agreement has not been reached. I may say that the fact that general elections have taken place in certain provinces during the summer and fall -this applies particularly to one province- may be the reason why the work of this

434	COMMONS
B.N.A. Act-Mr. Lapointe (Quebec East)
committee has not been concluded. May I suggest with all due deference to my hon. friend that the work he proposes should be done is of a delicate nature. It should be entrusted to a committee of legal experts rather than to a committee of members of the House of Commons. What can this committee do in addition to what was done in 1935? I have not heard one good reason advanced by my hon. friend in support of his resolution. He suggests that this committee would devise ways and means by which the will of the people, as represented in the House of Commons, would prevail. I believe that would be the one way to bring about greater friction with the provinces at a time when it is necessary to have agreement. We would have a committee composed of members of this house asserting that we must have this or we must have that, when in fact there are other parties who have something to say and something to do with this matter.
My hon. friend says that we have the Statute of Westminster which gives us more power and more rights. That may be so, but the provinces have exactly the same powers, the same rights and the same jurisdiction which they had prior to the passing of the Statute of Westminster. That is all reserved to them in the Statute of Westminster, and I do not think it could have gone through without those reservations. Until there has been a very great change in that respect, I cannot see how the Statute of Westminster would provide a good reason for the creation of a committee of this kind. While the Statute of Westminster may have changed the relations between the Dominion of Canada and the imperial parliament, it has not changed one iota the relations between the Dominion of Canada and the provinces of the confederation.
My hon. friend has said that this committee would define the respective powers of the dominion and the provinces. I have all the respect possible for the qualifications of the members of this proposed committee, but I am afraid that we must have more confidence in the decisions of the privy council and the Supreme Court of Canada. What could such a committee do except to read these decisions? It could not define powers and jurisdiction other than as they exist and as they have been defined by the courts. As I have stated in other circumstances, the fact of saying that we have jurisdiction does not give it. The assumption of powers which we do not have, does not give those powers to us. It will only make for greater difficulty

and not for the settlement of those questions, the settlement of which we all have so much at heart. I am afraid that instead of helping toward an agreement, this method would be more of an obstacle.
Those who sat on the committee in 1935-
I th'ink the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will agree to this-will agree with me when I say that provinces resented the fact that this committee was sitting. When the committee decided to summon the attorneys general and other officials of the provinces to present their views before it, they answered- and I think they answered properly

that they would deal as between government and government. They did not think the provinces, which were sovereign within their sphere, should be called upon to appear before a committee of the House of Commons. As I say, I think the provinces were right in making this answer.
I believe they would take the same position to-day. They would resent the fact that a committee of the House of Commons had started on the work of revising the constitution. As I have said, much more work will have to be done by way of negotiation and communication with the provinces. I think we are all in agreement as to the necessity of some amendment being made. I hope this will be done, but I repeat that it can be done only by securing the agreement of the provinces and not by asserting that we in the House of Commons can change the constitution of Canada by ourselves.
Canada is a confederation. My hon. friend referred to the greater ease of operation of unitary governments. No doubt he is right about that, but our constitutional situation is the result of conditions which prevail in Canada. Unless those powers had been left to the provinces they would never have agreed to come into confederation, and let me repeat again what I have said on a similar motion. The dominion is the child of the provinces; it is not their father. The provinces were in existence, had their powers, had their jurisdiction; they agreed to depart from a certain portion of their powers provided they were left with jurisdiction in other spheres, and they would never have come in and formed this Canada as it is if there had not been agreement at the conference which took place and which resulted in the British North America Act, a statute which was passed in England, that those provincial powers should remain within the sphere of authority of the provinces.

B.NA. Act-Mr. Pelletier
I repeat that what remains to be done is indeed very, very delicate work, and I do not see, with all deference to my hon. friend, that the committee which he suggests would in any way help the solution of the problem w'hich we want settled.

subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking to this motion may I at the outset lay down two rules which must be fully grasped and appreciated if the remarks that are to follow are to convey clearly and concisely the necessity of carrying out the request made in this resolution.
The first rule is this:	The vitality of national life, being dependent upon the harmony of its component parts, is capable of resisting temporal erosion in proportion to the degree in which harmony exists.
The second ride is: The deterioration of a political entity, subject to the diversity of its constituent elements, is slow or rapid in proportion to the fractional facets of its local problems.
With these thoughts in mind I had placed on the order paper a resolution which calls for the establishment of a commission to investigate the circumstances and problems of western Canada. I firmly believe that the resolution now before us is out of place, because before we can be in a position to amend the British North America Act, we must first find out what the problems demanding solution are, and this cannot be done until the problems affecting various parts of the country are studied. In my resolution I suggest a commission to investigate conditions in western Canada simply because I feel that before we attempt to amend the British North America Act, we should know what is the trouble with us. Therefore, in speaking to the resolution before us, I shall take up particularly western Canadian problems because there is a possibility that my resolution on the order paper may not be reached this session.
On March 29. 1867, the British North America Act received royal assent, and it became operative by royal proclamation on July 1, 1867. The purpose of this act, we must assume, was first of all to benefit all parts of the British North American colonies through legislation passed by the central government and designed to increase commerce. In the debates of the house in 1879, at page 429, we find Sir Leonard Tilley making the following statement:
The time has arrived. I think, when it will become our duty to decide whether the thousands of men throughout the length and breadth of this country who are unemployed, shall seek 31111-28^
employment in another country, or shall find it in this dominion; the time has arrived when we are to decide whether we will be simply hewers of wood and drawers of water; whether we will be simply agriculturists raising wheat, and lumbermen producing more lumber than we can use or Great Britain and the United States will take from us at remunerative prices; whether we will confine our attention to the fisheries and certain other small industries, and cease to be what we have been, and not rise to be what I believe we are destined to be under wise and judicious legislation, or -whether we will inaugurate a policy that will, by its provisions, say to the industries of the country, we will give you sufficient protection; we will give you a market for what you can produce; we will say that, while our neighbours build up a Chinese wall, we will impose a reasonable duty on their products coming into this country; at all events, we will maintain for our agricultural and other productions largely, the market of our own dominion.
Second, as is shown by the records of that time, on the insistence of the British Colonial Office there was an attempt to meet the policy of defence of the imperial government. With this second reason we are not for the moment greatly concerned. In any event the western provinces are now within the scope of confederation, and their entry must necessarily have been harmonious with the hope expressed by Sir Leonard Tilley.
In 1856 the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, comprising an area of 2,000,000 square miles, contained 6,691 persons in addition to the Indians. Less than 9,000 acres of land were under cultivation. Fifteen years later, in the same area the population had increased to 73.228, and ten years later to 122,400, with 279,249 acres under cultivation.
The policy of the Canadian government at that time was that expansion of settlement westward was logical and desirable, and that the agricultural possibilities of the country were too great to admit of its being reserved any longer for the fur trade. The settlement of the western Canadian plains was a clean-cut experiment in agricultural colonization. Thus we find that between 1897 and 1905, under the Hon. Clifford Sifton, the west developed at an amazing rate. Our immigration propaganda in the United States, Great Britain and Europe was most vigorous. For example, the report of immigration for 1904, part 2, at page 16, shows that no less than 2,703,646 pamphlets were sent out. These were issued not in the English language alone, but in French, German, Dutch, Norwegian and Swedish. The idea was to attract immigrants and to develop western Canada as rapidly as possible. It is plainly seen to-day in what manner this has affected the problems
B.N.A. Act-Mr. Pelletier

of the west. Settlers were encouraged to go west, but not with any particular guidance. Settlements sprung up rapidly. The inducements were great, and thousands trekked to western Canada and settled where they desired.
During the sixty years in which the Canadian northwest has been part of Canada its population has increased from 73,000 to 2,354,000, and the improved acres of land have increased from 279.000 in 1881 to 59,854,000 in 1931, out of 109,778,000 acres of occupied land. While this increase was fostered wholly by the federal government, no thought was given at the time to the problems which eventually must be faced by the provincial governments in regard to roads. Secluded areas had to be linked. Hundreds of miles of roads had to be built, and to-day a large part of the obligations of the western provinces may be traced directly to capital outlays for road construction.
It is perhaps unusual to ask a federal government to realize how it could in any measure be responsible for capital outlays made by autonomous and responsible legislative assemblies, but one must remember that the spirit of expansion and development was bred into western settlers' minds by federal immigration policies, and those settlers, of course, insisted and still insist upon more and more roads. Thus it would seem to me that out of the experiences of the past a better method of settlement could be worked out. For example, certain areas of land now sparsely settled could be considered by both provincial and federal governments as " prospective settlement districts." These districts should be permitted to be settled only under a definite settlement scheme. The area could be thoroughly surveyed and settlement permitted only at certain points agreed upon by both provincial and federal governments. The type of settlers could be chosen. Roads could be built only where necessary.
The northern portions of the western provinces all contain land, which some day will be settled. Even to-day settlers are being taken out of dried out areas and dumped somewhere in the northern bush, in places almost impossible of access. Of course these settlers want roads; they are entitled to them and the roads should be built. However, this entails hundreds of miles of roads for a small population. This expense could be lessened without suffering to anyone, always providing, however, that foresight and judgment are used.

The methods of colonization have resulted in bringing about unbearable financial difficulties to the western provinces, and if a commission is set up, this grievance can be thoroughly investigated. I feel sure that a remedy would be found.
Another source of ill feeling in western Canada is the present structure of freight rates. It is true that, owing to substantially low rates on grain, grain-growing in western Canada has been helped, but to-day the situation is not the same. In days gone by, many people settled in the west simply with the idea of attempting to make a fortune raising wheat; they were wheat miners. After making a fortune, it was their intention to return to eastern Canada to live. This is no longer the case. The people of the west have come to think of western Canada as home and as a result have become engaged to an increasing degree in producing other commodities than wheat alone.
When it is generally admitted that substantially low rates on grain had a beneficial effect, surely similar rates applied to western production would work the same way and would be beneficial in more than one respect. They would encourage mixed farming which, in the final analysis, is the best and safest method of assuring a degree of security to western farmers. Mixed farming means many things. It promotes protection of farm land by necessitating crop rotation, more extensive growth of fodder crops, such as grasses, sweet clover, etcetera. It permits certain sections of land retaining wooded areas, a protection against drought. It supplies a ready market for grain and an income of some sort.
Furthermore, the west knows that competitive factors, both on the Pacific coast and in eastern Canada, have compelled basically lower freight rates in those two sections of the country, but in the case of the prairie provinces no comparative basic change of freight rates has taken place for the last twenty-two or twenty-three years. Also eastern Canada, being older than the west, naturally has better roads. This fact has encouraged transportation by truck and bus to a degree sufficient to compel revision of railway rates in many instances.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reason I am mentioning these matters is that before we can intelligently discuss amendments to the British North America Act, certain problems must be pointed out and certain remedies proposed for them. It is impossible to amend the British North America Act unless we know what it is about, and I believe these matters are in line with the resolution.
I should like to quote the freight on a few items, so as to give a clear idea of what I have in mind. Let us take dry goods, for example. The distance from Montreal to Calgary is 2,324 miles. The freight for 100 pounds of dry goods in boxes is 19-04 cents per 100 pounds per 100 miles. On exactly the same dry goods in the same packages, shipped from Vancouver to Calgary, a distance of 641-5 miles, the rate per 100 pounds per 100 miles is 34-10 cents. The distance between Montreal and Winnipeg is 1,410-3 miles and the rate for dry goods in boxes per 100 pounds is S2.67J. The distance between Vancouver and Winnipeg is 1,473-02 miles, or 63 miles further than the distance between Montreal and Winnipeg, but the rate is $3.72 per 100 pounds. The cost for those extra 63 miles is S1.04i per 100 pounds.
These rates are supplied to me from an official source and were in effect on January 20 of this year. I have not attempted to compile a large set of figures, embodying various commodities, but the principle which governs freight rates in this particular instance also governs freight rates in others, and therefore, comparatively speaking, the same condition would be found to exist.
In any event, sixty per cent of the total freight revenue of the Canadian Pacific railway is derived from western Canada. These figures were quoted by President Beatty at the last meeting of the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. If for no other reason than that western Canada provides the most freight revenue, it is entitled to a hearing, and that reason alone would be sufficient. I am not, by any stretch of the imagination, touching upon all the various expressions of feeling heard in western Canada regarding freight rates. A commission would gather a wealth of material and give westerners an opportunity of "getting things off their chests."
I am also of opinion that the effect of Canada's tariff structure causes one of the most serious wrongs on western Canada. The west supplies the bulk of Canada's exports in the form of grain, cattle and lumber. Canada's industrial plant is in the east and of course industry requires some protection and obtains this protection but only at the expense of western Canada. Other nations are quick to retaliate by shutting out Canadian wheat, cattle and lumber.
The natural resources of the east, their earlier development than has been the case in the west, the water powers and the tariff have naturally concentrated manufacturing in Ontario and Quebec. Industrial development in the east has been a benefit to Canada as a whole. While one cannot disagree with the principle of the tariff, one must recognize the fundamental principle under confederation of the equal- right of all provinces; this, of course, can be worked out only under a general "give and take". In doing this and considering the tariff one must take into account the centres of manufacture in Ontario and Quebec; the long freight hauls to markets in the west; the barrier of the Rocky mountains, and the beneficial effects the west, through the construction and operation of the Panama canal, may have to trade with other countries.
Let us see what has been the outgrowth of the tariff policy in Canada. The only complete study of this matter was done by the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), and published in the report, "A Submission on Dominion-Provincial Relations and the Fiscal Disabilities of Nova Scotia within the Confederation," Province of Nova Scotia Royal Commission Economic Inquiry. subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was attempting to show that this resolution really does not cover what in my opinion is necessary in order to settle some of our difficulties as far as the constitution of Canada is concerned. Continuing, I would say that owing to the variety of interests in our dominion, in both the political and the economic spheres, these expressions of a desire for betterment have not been identical in all provinces. People in some provinces think assistance would be forthcoming if a certain thing were done. People in other provinces, facing the same problem, because of local factors believe that the difficulty can be best solved in some other manner, thus bringing about that ever present conflict between the provincial legislatures and this parliament in the exercise of their constitutional jurisdictions. Thus it is most difficult to .find any point of mutual agreement that would form a basis for a conference such as has been suggested by my hon. friend.
This was definitely proved when the Prime Minister read from the report of the 1935 committee on the British North America Act, before which Doctor Beauchesne recommended a convention to draft a new constitution. In that report, as the Prime Minister pointed out. the views of the various provinces are brought to the surface, and they indicate utter lack of mutual agreement with regard to any one suggested change. In almost every instance a desire for change was expressed, but nowhere do we find agreement as to what changes should be made. In Canada to-day we find a restlessness which is becoming alarming. Discontent, discord, lack of stability and uneasiness, prevail. No
one knows what may happen next. There is nothing solid. That is how people feel, but in my opinion we have something solid; we have our constitution.
I come back to a rule which I laid down in my opening remarks. That is, the vitality of national life, being dependent upon the harmony of its component parts, is capable of resisting temporal erosion in proportion to the degree in which harmony exists. At the moment harmony does not exist. At the moment in the west people live in the shadow of wrongs, either fancied or real. They fancy that eastern Canada does not understand them. On the other hand the people of eastern Canada feel that the west is a burden; they picture western Canadians as individuals who are forever running to the federal treasury for loans. They fancy that the east pays the bills while the west lives in irresponsible affluence. The west resents this attitude. It knows that factors beyond its control took away its purchasing power by immensely reducing its income from the growing of grain. It knows how it has suffered through drought, hot winds, grasshoppers, hail and frost. It feels its wounds, not because they hurt but because they bring no sympathy. The west is part of Canada; it is the child of the east, and now that adolescent child is abandoned to lick its salty sores and whimper alone. The guns of Europe might rumble once more. Perhaps that would be important to Canada, but of greater importance still is that slow-burning fire of distress which leads to hate smouldering in this Canadian family. The child of the east cries out; it extends its hands in earnest desire for friendly cooperation and justice. Let the east awaken and reply in kind and encourage us so that we in whom Canadians have placed their confidence may fail not. Let us, within the framework of our constitution, our solid constitution, offer that opportunity of expression which must result in dispelling distrust and bring back once more the harmony which is so essential to the survival of this nation.
Let us give the west a hearing. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, certain things that have happened in western Canada have resulted from the conditions I have mentioned to-day. It seems to me that if we attempt to remedy the situation by amending the British North America Act we must know first of all what it is we are seeking to do and how to go about securing the desired result. It seems to me that a commission or a committee of this house, empowered to look into these problems in Canada, could not

B.NA. Act-Mr. Woodsworth
possibly arrive at sound conclusions or discover the correct answers unless first it knew exactly what it was looking for. We do not need any further proof of that than what recently happened in western Canada, as far as the expression of public opinion is concerned. As I have said already, we hear all sorts of expressions of opinion, and I believe many of them originate simply through the failure of the federal government to give effect to laws which are demanded by the man in the street. We find that he must have some medium of expression, and that medium has not been provided by the federal government. So he has turned his attention to the provincial legislatures and has forced them to enact laws some of which come into conflict or are said to come into conflict with our federal laws.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I trust that the government will take into serious consideration the points I have brought out. Western Canada is an essential and a great part of Canada, and I believe that in its desire to maintain confederation, seeking cooperation and desiring assistance, it will receive that help and that cooperation which I know this parliament can give.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to
associate myself with my colleague the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) in urging the government to consider seriously the appointment of such a committee. I recall that I introduced a motion of this kind as far back as 1924, and again in 1931. Two years ago, in 1935, I brought forward another motion, a little different, a little more limited in scope, which was referred to a committee, to which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) referred this afternoon. My motion read:
That, in the opinion of this house, a special committee should be set up to study and report on the best method by which the British North America Act may be amended so that while safeguarding the existing rights of racial and religious minorities and legitimate provincial claims to autonomy, the dominion government may be given adequate power to deal effectively with urgent economic problems which are essentially national in scope.
In presenting that resolution I was careful to assure the house that there was no thought in my mind of interfering with any of the existing rights of the provinces, and I tried especially to safeguard the rights of racial and religious minorities.
The house received that resolution very favourably, and the committee, I think I may say, worked quite conscientiously in endeavour-

ing to find some way by which we could amend our constitution. However, the committee failed lamentably, because of a lack of cooperation with the provinces, and I believe, behind that, because of the assumption that we must have the consent of all the provinces before we could take any action. So the committee brought in finally what I must confess was a milk and water sort of report, suggesting that this whole matter should be referred to a dominion-provincial conference.
The resolution that has been placed before us to-day is somewhat different. It suggests that a parliamentary committee should study and report upon the specific amendments which might be brought in to meet the outstanding needs of our country at this time. The committee which sat two years ago dealt with the method. This time we have approached the matter in a different way, urging that the committee at least might survey the field and suggest the particular changes needed to meet the urgent problems which face us to-day. I regret that the government has not seen its way to accede to our request, and to appoint such a committee. I regret even more, however, that the Minister of Justice, who spoke for the government, has offered no alternative.
I shall not attempt again to traverse the ground so well covered by my colleague from Rosetown-Biggar, but may I venture to call to the attention of the house, a house which since 1935 is partly new, several considerations I tried to emphasize in 1935. Why should we not have an amendment to our constitution? The then Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), during the debate in the house on April 13, 1934, made this statement:
Two answers could be given to that question; one is the political answer and the other is the legal answer. The legal answer is that if this parliament-and that means both houses-adopts a resolution embodying a petition to the sovereign for the enactment of legislation by the parliament at Westminster amending the British North America Act, under the Statute of Westminster such legislation would be enacted accordingly.
I believe there can be no question that that is a fair statement of the situation. It seemed to me that this afternoon the Minister of Justice rather receded from the position which was common two years ago in this chamber. It seemed to me that he was going back to the old idea that there exists a sort of treaty between the provinces and the dominion and that we have to live up to that treaty. I hope I do not misrepresent him, but as he spoke this afternoon that was the im-

B.NA. Act-Mr. Woodsworth
pression I gathered. Again let me point out that as a matter of fact the British North America Act has actually been amended in various ways. It was once amended by the British parliament on the strength of a simple request by the Canadian government, without the proposal even coming before parliament. A great many people have the idea that the British North America Act is like the laws of the Medes and Persians, that it can never be changed. But we forget the very large number of amendments that have already been made in the act. Once a request which was made by the dominion parliament carried the formal endorsation of eight out of the nine provinces and was opposed by one province. On the other occasions the British parliament acted on the joint request of the Canadian House of Commons and the Senate. The precedents therefore suggest that the British parliament will enact any legislation to amend the British North America Act on the recommendation of the Canadian parliament.
If we are to wait until we have a dominion-provincial conference and until such conference unanimously adopts not only a method of amending the act but also the amendments which should be made, I am afraid we shall have to wait indefinitely.

Then there is another consideration we ought to keep in mind-the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) called attention to it in an interjection to-day-that we must have the consent of the Senate. It is true that parliament consists of the House of

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext: Does my hon. friend think he can change that by creating a committee of the house?

subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Oh, no; we do not suggest that. The minister is expecting the committee to do a great deal more than that for which the resolution calls. In emphasizing the point to which reference was made this afternoon I should like to quote no other than the leader of the opposition. In 1915, on the occasion of the Senate declining to agree to an address for an immediate change in representation in that chamber, he denounced the Senate. At page 2338 of Hansard of that year he referred to the upper house as an "irresponsible body which thwarted the will of democracy, as expressed by this House of Commons." Perhaps that is stronger language than I might use! However, all I want to say is that if the Senate attempts to block amendments which are generally desired, we shall have to find means of dealing with the Senate. That is all I need say at the moment, but I think it should be said.
Referring to a statement by my colleague the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, the Minister of Justice stated that the Statute of Westminster did not alter the relationships between the provinces and the dominion. I think we all agree with that. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar did not argue otherwise, but if I followed his argument it was this, that the parliament of Great Britain is sovereign. In Canada parliament has occupied a subordinate position. Under the Statute of Westminster Canada to-day is supposed to be as sovereign as the parliament of Great Britain. I think no one doubts that the parliament of Great Britain could alter the British North America Act, and conceivably could do so without an address from the two Canadian houses. It could make alterations in opposition to provincial representations. I do not assert that such action is likely, but I say the British North America Act is an imperial statute and can be altered by that imperial body. Since the passing of the Statute of Westminster the Canadian parliament ought to have an authority equal to that which exists in the imperial house. I believe that it was along these lines the hon. member was making his argument. If not, I take it as my own.

B.N.A. Act-Mr. Woodsworth
We cannot go on indefinitely under the arrangement that we must refer matters to some body other than our own. We have full authority here to deal with Canadian affairs. The thing that worried me this afternoon was not so much the suggestion of the minister that this matter could be dealt with better by some sort of commission-and I am getting a little tired of commissions composed largely of lawyers; I think we might very well get away from that kind of commission and have commissioners who represent a great many other interests in the dominion

and not so much that it could be dealt with by a dominion-provincial conference-that may be the best way to deal with it-but rather that the minister offers very little by way of an alternative to the existing situation. If he would give us a guarantee that the dominion-provincial conference will be called within six months and pledge his word that that conference will take action-

speechtext: How far is my hon. friend prepared to go in compromising with regard to his principles? That is always a point in connection with these conferences. I do not believe my hon. friend would compromise to any extent.

speechtext:
I hope my hon. friend is correct in his estimate of me. I have tried to make that my rule. However,
I think there are principles and principles. There are certain things which have been elevated to the position of principles, which are regarded by some people as being principles, but which have not universal application. It may be said that in this connection there are two principles at stake.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext: Judging by what the provinces say to us, there are many.

subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Fundamentally the principles at stake are certain rights of the provinces, certain powers known as provincial autonomy, and, on the other hand,

certain rights and powers of the dominion. It may be said that those two principles clash. That may be so, but my point is that we cannot let this situation go on forever, drift as it has done, without imperilling the whole of confederation.
Let me bring a further matter to the attention of the house. From my standpoint, the recent decisions of the judicial committee of the privy council were most unsatisfactory, if I may say so without getting into trouble with all the lawyers in this house. They are unsatisfactory from my standpoint because the privy council, sitting in England, cannot have the information and point of view that we have in Canada.

subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
They
agreed with the supreme court here.

subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
That is quite true. If we refused to send legal questions to the judicial committee of the privy council I think we would be a little bit more careful about the decisions given by the Supreme Court of Canada. If I might be permitted to say so, I think we would also be a little bit more careful as to the calibre of the judges we put in our supreme court. It would tend to throw greater responsibility upon our own institutions. I am not criticizing this or that or the other individual but I submit that as long as we remain in tutelage, as long as we look overseas for someone to tell us in the last analysis what must be done, we shall remain immature and all our decisions will be of a tentative nature. For one, I shall be very glad when we stand on our own two feet and recognize that we must work out our own problems right here in Canada.
I want to say one thing further in this connection. I belong to a province and I come from a section of this country which was not a party to the British North America Act. At the time that act was passed my people were all in eastern Canada and I had not been born, but as eastern Canada dealt with this matter it might be claimed that I must accept some responsibility. I come from Manitoba and I have lived most of my life in the west. We as a province, or as provinces, were not a party to the British North America Act and you could not possibly put over such an act to-day and have the west a party to it. I do not like threats, but I want to remind this house of the sporadic movements which have sprung up in the west from time to time looking in the direction of secession. These movements will spread unless action is taken in the not distant future. The west has reached a stage where it simply cannot carry on. One province has defaulted and in

B.N.A. Act-Mr. Woodsworth
all probability, unless some very special arrangements are made, it will not be very long before other western provinces default.
We find that there are certain ideals which are common to all four western provinces, but which apparently are not held by some of the provinces in the east. We want it understood that we cannot go on indefinitely suffering under certain disabilities which could be altered if we operated under another constitution. If the fathers of confederation whom we praise so highly had sense enough to get together and work out a constitution which no doubt was more or less fitted for their day, I urge that we are not worthy sons of theirs unless we in our day can get together and work out a constitution, different perhaps from the old one, which will serve the needs of our day.

speechtext: What changes would the hon. member suggest?

The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George can read it to-morrow in Hansard. Certain very definite changes are outlined in the resolution now before us and they deal largely with the social problems that face us.

My hon. friend behind me says that they are the changes advocated by the leader of the party of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. Let me read the resolution again:
-in view of the urgent necessity of effective action for the improvement of the social and economic conditions of the people of Canada-
Whether such action is needed in the community represented by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, I am not prepared to say.

subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext: Explain; social and economic conditions mean nothing definite.

subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
They do mean
something to me. Let me read this:
-in view of the conditions of social and other legislation passed by parliament during the tenure of office of the late government-
Does that mean nothing to my hon. friend? He was a member of that government. He knows how most of that legislation has gone by the board.

subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext: Did he approve and does he approve the method adopted by the late administration in acquiring that measure of jurisdiction which formerly had always been regarded as belonging to the provinces?

subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext: I do not know that I am required to answer whether or not I approved that legislation, especially in view of the fact that it has been thrown out by the judicial committee of the privy council as unconstitutional. But I do say that the things which were attempted by the previous government by way of certain measures to provide for unemployment insurance, the eight hour day and all the rest of it, were in my judgment highly desirable.

subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext: What of the means?

subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
I am asking that means be devised. The Minister of Labour gave evidence before the committee of a year ago and I think he is very well acquainted with certain means that might be attempted. We are not urging that this particular measure should be the only one before the house. As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar suggested, if this is not satisfactory, we shall be very glad to support any other measure which might be considered more satisfactory. But we want some measure.
A few minutes ago, I referred to secession, this not by way of a threat because I have always opposed secession movements on the ground that they were an attempted political solution for some of our great economic problems. But someone should point out that some sections of our country will be driven ultimately to attempt some such solution. We cannot go on in this way very much longer. We are urging that before things become too desperate, the situation in Canada should be saved.
I read several editorials following the decision of the judicial committee of the privy council. I want to read the opening paragraph of an editorial in the Montreal Gazette of January 30, 1937:
There is ground for a great deal of satisfaction on the part of Canadian business, as well as on the part of all minorities in 'this country, in the fact that the British North America Act has survived the efforts of a dominion parliament to shoot holes through it.
That was the opening paragraph, and I think it is wonderfully revealing. All minorities should rejoice in this, it says. Now my

B.N.A. Act-Mr. Woodsworth
own position with regard to minorities has been stated again and again. It was stated in that resolution which I brought into the house two years ago. Let me read it:
That, in the opinion of this house, a special committee should be set up to study and report on the best method by which the British North America Act may be amended so that while safeguarding the existing rights of racial and religious minorities and legitimate provincial claims to autonomy, the dominion government may be given adequate power to deal effectively with urgent economic problems which are essentially national in scope.
I have every respect for, and I want this country to safeguard carefully the racial and religious rights of minorities, but on the other hand I do not believe that a minority, even a racial or religious minority, must be allowed to hold up progress in this country. I should like some time to talk on the rights of majorities.

subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext: Page Mr. Rowe.

subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
No; I am no religious fanatic, and anybody who knows me recognizes that I am no fanatic so far as language or anything of that kind is concerned, but I do say this, that the majorities in this dominion have certain rights and we must not forever be held down by the ideals of one or two or three or five particular sections of the community. In reality I am not so much concerned with racial and religious minorities as I am with some other kinds of minorities. I am thinking of financial minorities, and I am thinking of some industrialists in this country, small groups of people who for their own ends ask that progress be delayed. It is from this standpoint that I read this opening paragraph in the Gazette:
There is ground for a great deal of satisfaction on the part of Canadian business, as well as on the part of all minorities-*
The Gazette is published in Montreal, and it is perhaps a good political move to stir up a little bit of racial antagonism in that way. It may catch the people of Montreal or the people of Quebec; it may catch some here, there or yonder; I do not know. I repeat, I stand for the rights of minorities, racial or religious. But when the Gazette says that this is a matter for great satisfaction to Canadian business, I cannot but think of resolutions that have been sent to me during the fifteen years I have been in this house, as well as editorials I have read, in which Canadian business, that is organized big business, has done its best to thwart eight hour day legislation, to thwart the minimum wage legislation, to thwart old age pensions, to thwart unemployment insurance. Canadian

business has been again and again opposed to these things. On occasion they would say: We are British. When we have pointed out that in Great Britain they have social legislation of this kind, and have had it for years, " Oh well," they reply, " that is different." They back away from their patriotism then, and a cheap patriotism it is, too, when you put it up to them. For years they came to our committees and said, " We cannot do anything because we have to compete with the great republic to the south of us. They have no eight-hour day in many of the states, no unemployment insurance, no sickness insurance; so we cannot do anything at the present time in Canada." Now a large measure of social security legislation has been enacted in the United States, and yet here in Canada we have Canadian workers, in the steel plants, working, I am credibly informed, thirteen hours at night when we have vast numbers of unemployed. We cannot do anything to alter the situation because the British North America Act stands in the way. We have five thousand families unemployed in my city, and have had them for years. They are growing old in receiving relief. These people should have had unemployment insurance years ago, but when we propose it we are told: " We cannot do	anything-the	British North
America Act!" And Canadian business rejoices because the British North America Act blocks any legislation of the kind. These are the matters to which we ought to pay some attention. But the Gazette says:
There is ground for a great deal of satisfaction on the part of Canadian business, as well as on the part of all minorities in this country, in the fact that the British North America Act has survived the efforts of a dominion parliament to shoot holes through it.
Was there anything in the legislation proposed by the late government two years ago, in regard to the eight-hour day, unemployment insurance and all the rest of it, that took away the rights of minorities? Not that I know of. We all agree that these things should be done, and the British North America Act is just a herring across the trail. What we really have to face is a certain class of people in this country who will stand behind this old document seventy years of age and prevent us from progressing on to better things.
This government should be given a chance to determine its action. I did not expect any action last year, because it was the first year of a new government in power, but when we come this year and urge that some-

B.N.A. Act-Mr. Rogers
thing be done, about all that we get from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), representing the government, is simply an enumeration of a number of difficulties in the way.

Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour): I wish to speak briefly to this resolution and in support of the objections to its adoption which were expressed so clearly this afternoon by my colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). The mover of the resolution in his concluding remarks made the novel and refreshing suggestion that he would be quite prepared to withdraw it if he could be convinced that there was some better way of dealing with a constitutional amendment at this time. Perhaps he is already convinced that there is a better way; at all events, I am going to take him at his word, and shall try to indicate the reasons why in my opinion this resolution is inopportune and unacceptable at this time.	.
My first objection to the resolution is this: No investigation by a special committee of this house and no resolution of this house can promote or expedite the amendment of the British North America Act. We may declare here that the dominion parliament ought to have jurisdiction over hours and wages and unemployment insurance, but this declaration would not of itself bring us any closer to the realization of that objective. The question of how the proposed amendments would be given effect would still remain unsettled.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext: That is the point.

subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND AMENDMENTS LOOKING TO IMPROVEMENT OF SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS
speechtext:
That question, as was
pointed out by the Minister of Justice this afternoon, can be determined only by consultation and cooperation between the dominion and the provinces, and it has already been brought to the attention of this house that such consultation and such cooperation are now in progress.
The truth of the matter is-and I am quite sure it is known to most members of this house-that we do not possess in Canada at this time any recognized procedure for the amendment of our own constitution. So far as I am aware the Canadian constitution is the only federal constitution the world over which suffers from this particular infirmity. It is perhaps only of antiquarian interest to seek to determine wrhy it was that there was this great omission in the original terms of the British North America Act. There are some who suggest that the omission was simply a matter of inadvertence. There are others who contend that the omission was deliberate. I am bound to say that there is a body of evidence to support each point of view. But that particular question does not concern us now. We are confronted with this situation, that, the British North America Act does not
B.NA. Act-Mr. Rogers

of itself contain any procedure for its own amendment. Any recommendations that might be made by a select committee of this house would be nothing more than recommendations. As I suggested a moment ago, they would not of themselves advance the amendment of the British North America Act.
There are different opinions as to how we could proceed to develop a mechanism for the amendment of the British North America Act. Indeed I think the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) will admit that the determination of the procedure by which we shall amend the British North America Act is of more vital importance than the determination of specific amendments which may be made at any given point of time. And even if a select committee of this house were able to agree that the dominion parliament ought to have jurisdiction over hours and wages and unemployment insurance, we would still be faced with the necessity of consulting with the provinces and seeking to secure from them an agreement as to the precise measure of consultation and agreement which would be required in order to enact these amendments. Upon that question, as was said a moment ago by the hon member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), there is a divergence of opinion in this country. There are those, for example, who contend that the British North America Act, lacking as it does any specific procedure of amendment, can be amended only when all the provinces have given consent to any proposal for amendment. There are those on the contrary who have suggested that the dominion .parliament should of itself propose amendments, as has been done in times past, and that a joint address of the two houses of parliament at Ottawa should be a sufficient basis upon which the amendment to the British North America Act could be grounded. Between those two extreme views you have another view that there should be the assent of the two houses of the dominion parliament, in the form of an address, and at least some measure of approval by the various provincial legislatures. But that vexed question has yet to be determined, and in advance of its determination I do not see that any select committee of this House of Commons could serve a useful purpose at this time in proposing specific amendments to the British North America Act.
My second objection to the resolution is this:	In view of the recent decisions of the
privy council it would be more appropriate, and probably more effective, to give the provinces an opportunity to take the initiative in proposing specific constitutional

amendments at this time. In support of this contention it will be necessary to remind the house of the sequence of events which led to the far-reaching decisions of the privy council which were announced last week. Until January, 1935, it was generally assumed in this dominion that exclusive jurisdiction over hours and wages and unemployment insurance lay with the provinces. As a matter of fact I remember reading a report of a most interesting address by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) which was delivered in the month of November preceding January, 1935, in which he stated in the most vigorous terms that no lawyer doubted that the exclusive jurisdiction over these matters lay with the provincial legislatures. How was it, then, that despite the view of the courts of this country and of legal practitioners generally we find the dominion parliament assuming a jurisdiction over these matters which everyone had supposed belonged to the provinces? I do not think I misrepresent the situation when I say that this astonishing change came about as a result of a decision which was reached by the then Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Bennett). Early in September of 1934 the present leader of the opposition went to Geneva. I suggest that on his way to or from Geneva he saw a great light. As events have proved, it was a false and deceptive light, and with his wide knowledge of law and history he ought to have known that it was a false and deceptive light. But he chose to accept its guidance, and because he accepted its guidance we find ourselves in the position to-day of having a definition of provincial rights in respect to these matters which to some extent, I think, goes further than any decisions have gone in previous years.

speechtext:
With great deference to his legal knowledge, I beg to differ with my hon. friend on that point. The violence of the attack on provincial autonomy and the arbitrary method employed by the present leader of the opposition in his invasion of provincial jurisdiction had the natural result of placing the provinces on the defensive, and accentuated their determination to maintain their autonomy before the courts. As a consequence it would seem that the decisions of the privy council as announced last week have gone further in emphasizing and entrenching provincial rights than any decisions given for many years. Indeed, I think I may at least express this view, that when the decisions come to us, if they bear out the newspaper reports already published, it will be found that this country is going to be more fettered in respect to certain phases of its external relations than it has been hitherto. In other words, I believe it is possible to say that the counter-attack has been more successful than the attack. Instead of gaining ground the dominion government has lost ground; instead of enlisting the cooperation of the provinces, the method adopted has thrown a cloud of suspicion and distrust over the field of dominion-provincial relations, and instead of reconciliation there has been recrimination and at least a measure of reaction.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that this attempt of the late administration to use section 132 of the British North America Act as a means of amending the constitution-for it was that-has produced some of these results I have indicated and has actually left dominion-provincial relations in a less satisfactory state than before. One fact at least has been established; it is the one cause for satisfaction which can be salvaged from this episode. We now know, if there was any uncertainty before, that exclusive jurisdiction over hours, wages and unemployment insurance lies with the provincial legislatures; all doubts upon this point have been dispelled. But I want to suggest that it has cost us something to have these doubts removed; it has cost us far more than was necessary. It would have cost a vastly greater sum if the leader of the opposition had carried out his original intention and had built up an elaborate civil service organization to administer the several statutes which now have been declared invalid by the highest court of appeal. We heard, only a few days ago of members of the Employment and Social Insurance Commission who, because of the recent decisions of the privy council, find themselves without
employment. In 1935 an order in council was passed which contemplated something in the neighbourhood of one hundred key positions under the Employment and Social Insurance Act. This did not begin to include the clerical positions which would have been established across this country had that act been put fully into effect. What it would have cost individuals and business enterprises to adjust and readjust their operations to these invalid statutes is beyond calculation.
There is an old maxim that it is well to forgive and forget. I am quite willing, as we must all be willing, to forgive; but I think, in the interests of this country, we ought not to forget this particular transaction. What has happened and what has been avoided should serve as a warning to all governments against forsaking the tried and proved foundations of constitutional usage for the shifting sands of political expediency. I shall say no more on this question.

We are now, however, confronted with a situation which at least is fairly definite.
That brings me to the second objection I take to the resolution which is now before the house. The provinces possess the jurisdiction to deal with labour and social legislation. This jurisdiction cannot be taken from them by violence or by any declaration that can be made by this parliament. It will not, in the light of existing judicial decisions, be transferred to the dominion parliament by the process of judicial interpretation. It can be given to the dominion parliament, in whole or in part, only by an act of voluntary surrender of jurisdiction by the provincial legislatures. The initiative, in other words, now lies with the provinces themselves.
It has already been brought to the attention of the house that an effort has been made through a dominion-provincial conference to determine the procedure by which the British North America Act shall be amended in future years. This resolution, however, appears to contemplate something in addition to that, namely, the adoption of a number of specific amendments here and now as a result of which jurisdiction over social legislation might be transferred from the provincial legislatures to the dominion parliament. I have had a very brief experience of dominion-provincial conferences. I happened to be present
44S
B.NA. Act-Mr. Rogers

as a member of the secretariat at the conference of 1927, and I have attended two or three dominion-provincial conferences during the past year. I do not think it would be unfair or in any way unreasonable to suggest that sometimes these conferences have failed because they have met in an atmosphere of suspicion and excessive caution. At times there appears to be a feeling on the part of the provinces that the dominion government has some ulterior object in view whenever specific proposals are made to them. At all events we do know that dominion-provincial conferences from time to time have not been as successful as we could have wished. I agree wholly with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in that observation. But I wonder whether, in view of the recent decis-sions of the privy council, the initiative does not now belong with the provinces.
Would any useful end be served at this time by the dominion parliament concurring in the report of a select committee proposing to the provincial legislatures that they should abandon some portion of their jurisdiction over social questions? After all, any doubts which may have existed before have now been resolved; the provinces possess the jurisdiction. Would it not be more reasonable to leave it to an interprovincial conference, if you will, to go into this question of whether certain measures of social legislation can be carried out more effectively by uniform action on the part of the provincial legislatures or by action of the dominion parliament? A few days ago it was said that public opinion in this country is tending more strongly in the direction of supporting more social legislation, and also supporting the view that such legislation should be enacted by the dominion parliament. I wonder why that public opinion could not be focussed also upon provincial legislatures, so that they might of themselves, without any compulsion, without any undue pressure from the dominion government, voluntarily surrender their jurisdiction in some respects to the dominion parliament.
It would not be the first time the question of constitutional amendments has been dealt with by an interprovincial conference as distinguished from a dominion-provincial conference. As a matter of fact, the first conference which was held after confederation was a conference of that kind. It was summoned by Mr. Mercier, then premier of Quebec, acting in close cooperation with Sir Oliver Mowat, then premier of Ontario. As a result of its deliberations that conference actually did propose a number of specific amendments to the British North America Act. It is not necessary to go into the history of

those resolutions. As a matter of fact, they fell by the wayside. They were sent to the imperial parliament with the suggestion that apart entirely from the views of the dominion parliament they should be enacted as amendments to the British North America Act, but it was represented to the imperial government of the day that this conference did not speak for Canada as a whole and that the dominion government would take strong exception to any attempt on the part of the imperial parliament to enact those resolutions as amendments to the British North America Act.
My point is simply this, that there is nothing to prevent the provinces from meeting together and discussing, in the light of the recent privy council decision, what they will do and how far they are prepared to go in adopting uniform statutes to deal, let us say, with hours of labour and wages; or, if they are not so prepared, to agree among themselves that they will transfer this jurisdiction to the dominion parliament.
My third objection to the resolution before the house, Mr. Speaker, is this: The mover of the resolution seems to have assumed that substantial amendments to the British North America Act are necessary in order to obtain adequate measures of social security in this country. I doubt if that assumption is wholly justified. I share entirety his view that owing largely to the increasing hazards associated with the changing character of economic life we must go further in the direction of social security than we have gone hitherto, but I do not think it follows of necessity that the sole responsibility for erecting that structure of social security should fall upon the dominion parliament. Clearly, the main object is to realize certain of these purposes, to remove as many as possible of these hazards or to afford protection against them, but I believe it quite possible and perhaps desirable that, particularly in a country of this kind, the framework should include legislation passed by different legislative bodies. At the present time practically all provincial legislatures have passed enactments providing for mothers' allowances and for workmen's compensation. Municipalities in some provinces have cooperated with respect to mothers' allowances and old age pensions. In the case of old age pensions there is a division of financial responsibility, though the legislation itself was enacted by this parliament. Already one province has embarked upon a measure of health insurance and another province has upon its statute books an act providing for state medicine, though as yet it has not been proclaimed.

B.NA.. Act-Mr. Cahan
After all, we must recognize that within a federal constitution we do have a collection of political entities; we do have a division of obligation and of powers. I do not think it follows of necessity, therefore, that in order to achieve these social objectives we must enact far-reaching amendments to the Canadian constitution. Much requires to be done in the way of a survey of the whole field in order that each may know what it can do efficiently. I am not suggesting that the dominion parliament ought not to have some powers which it does not now possess, but as I said a moment ago I do not think it follows that substantial amendments are necessary in order to carry out the objectives the mover of the resolution has in mind.
Let me speak for one moment of the United States; the hon. member referred to the social security program in that country. That program has not been carried through by a transfer of jurisdiction from the states to congress. In the main it has been carried out as a result of financial assistance being given by congress to the states providing that particular measures of social security enacted by the states conform to standards laid down by congress.
